title_en: A Fair Trial for the Four-Day Week
description_ru: Взвешенное эссе в защиту пилотных проектов с четырёхдневной неделей: аргументы сторонников, возражения скептиков и что показывают эксперименты.
text:
The five-day working week is so familiar that we tend to forget it was ever controversial. In 1926, Henry Ford announced that his factories would close on Saturdays as well as Sundays, and the business establishment predicted disaster. Instead, Ford's productivity held up, his workers had more time to buy and drive cars, and within a decade the two-day weekend had become a standard of civilised employment. I mention this history not because it proves that history will repeat itself, but because it should make us humble about our assumptions. A convention that looks permanent is often merely old.

Today the same question is being asked about a fourth day of rest. Over the past few years, trials in countries as different as Iceland, Britain, Portugal and Japan have tested a shorter working week, typically with no reduction in pay. The largest British pilot, involving around sixty companies and nearly three thousand employees, reported that the overwhelming majority of the firms chose to continue the arrangement afterwards. Revenue was broadly stable, resignations fell sharply, and workers described lower stress and better sleep. Naturally, such results have been seized upon by enthusiasts, and just as naturally, they have been dismissed by sceptics. I want to argue that both camps are getting ahead of the evidence, and that the sensible response is neither to adopt the policy blindly nor to reject it out of hand, but to give it a fair trial.

Consider the enthusiasts first, because they have a good deal on their side. The central insight is that hours worked and work achieved are not the same thing. Anyone who has sat through a pointless meeting, answered emails that could have been a sentence or watched a colleague arrange the appearance of busyness will recognise that much of the traditional working week is padding. When time is scarce, people discover that a meeting can last twenty minutes, that a report needs fewer pages and that half of the interruptions they thought essential were habits. In several of the trials, managers reported that the shorter week had forced them to confront inefficiencies that had been tolerated for years.

There are also persuasive human arguments. Exhausted employees make mistakes, and tired surgeons and drivers are a danger to the rest of us. A day off allows time for medical appointments, childcare and the tedious errands that otherwise swallow the weekend, reducing what some researchers call time poverty. The arrangement may even help to narrow the gender gap, since women still perform most unpaid domestic work, and a free weekday gives fathers an opportunity to share it. Employers, for their part, have noticed that a shorter week is an inexpensive way to attract talent in a competitive market, which may be the most convincing evidence of all, since few managers are motivated by sentiment.

Now for the sceptics, who also deserve a fair hearing. The first problem is selection. The firms that volunteer for pilot schemes are, by definition, enthusiastic, and their managers are likely to be flexible, well organised and keen to see the experiment succeed. A software company with a clear set of deliverables can compress its schedule; a hospital ward or a restaurant, where service depends on physical presence, cannot compress a night shift. A policy that works for knowledge workers may be unworkable, or may create new inequalities, for people who serve customers in person.

The second problem is intensity. Some employees in the trials reported that the same volume of work now had to be squeezed into four days, leaving them tired in a different way. If a shorter week merely produces a more frantic one, the gain in wellbeing may prove illusory, and a drop in stress could be followed by burnout. Anyone who has ever tried to complete a week's labour in four days will know that there is a ceiling to the concentration one can sustain.

A third objection concerns the long term. A pilot lasting six months captures the novelty and enthusiasm of the first phase, when everybody is determined to prove that the idea works. It tells us much less about what happens in the third year, when the glow has faded, a competitor has launched an aggressive campaign and the founder who believed in the scheme has moved on. Productivity, as economists remind us, is difficult to measure even in ordinary times.

So what should be done? I would suggest that the proper response is to be more rigorous, not less. Governments could encourage larger and longer trials, preferably with a randomly selected comparison group of firms that continue as before, in order to separate the effects of the policy from the effects of enthusiasm. Different sectors should be studied separately, and the measures should include not only revenue and sick days but also customer satisfaction, the quality of public services and the experiences of the colleagues who cover for others. The trials should be published whether or not they succeed.

There is something faintly absurd about a society that will spend years debating a motorway but treats the shape of the week, which affects every working person, as an immutable fact of nature. It is not. The week is a human invention, borrowed from religious tradition and adjusted by industrial bargaining, and it can be altered, when the evidence is strong, by human choice.

Perhaps the four-day week will prove a triumph; perhaps it will turn out to suit some industries and not others; perhaps it will join the long list of fashionable ideas that dissolved on contact with reality. I do not know, and neither, honestly, does anyone else. But I am quite sure that Henry Ford's critics were wrong to assume that the existing arrangement was the best one conceivable, and that we would be equally wrong to assume that today's is.

questions.question: What did Henry Ford do in 1926?
questions.answer: He closed his factories on Saturdays as well as Sundays.

questions.question: What did the large British pilot report?
questions.answer: Most firms continued; revenue stable, fewer resignations, less stress.

questions.question: What is the selection problem?
questions.answer: Firms that volunteer for trials are likely to be flexible and keen for it to succeed.

questions.question: What does the writer recommend?
questions.answer: Larger, longer, more rigorous trials with comparison groups.
